questiontext.text: In the SRTBOT questions, what does the letter B ask about?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. B stands for base cases, such as dp[0] = 0 and dp[1] = 1 in Fibonacci. Without them the recurrence has nothing to start from.

questiontext.text: Why is the plain recursive Fibonacci slow for large n ?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Each call spawns two more, and the same states are solved over and over, so the number of calls grows exponentially.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: It recomputes the same values again and again

questiontext.text: Why do we set ways[0] = 1 when counting the ways to climb stairs?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Counting adds up ways. If the base were 0, every number built from it would also be 0.

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
int coin[] = {1, 3, 4};
int amount = 6;
vector<int> dp(amount + 1, 1000);
dp[0] = 0;
for (int x = 1; x <= amount; x++) {
    for (int c : coin) {
        if (c <= x) {
            dp[x] = min(dp[x], dp[x - c] + 1);
        }
    }
}
cout << dp[amount] << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The best way to make 6 is 3 + 3, so two coins. A greedy choice that takes the biggest coin first (4 + 1 + 1) would need three coins, but the table finds the real minimum.

Uses addition (+): The number of different routes, How many ways to climb the stairs, How many ways to tile a strip

name.text: Q15 - Drag and drop - fill the gaps

questiontext.text:
Drag the correct pieces into the gaps so the program prints 8.

main.cpp
vector<long long> ways(6, 0);
ways[[[1]]] = 1;
for (int i = 1; i < 6; i++) {
    ways[i] = ways[i - 1] [[2]] (i >= 2 ? ways[i - 2] : 0);
}
cout << ways[5] << endl;

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. The base case belongs at index 0. Counting ways adds the ways of the two previous cells, giving 1 1 2 3 5 8. With the base at index 1 the loop would overwrite it with 0 and everything stays 0.

The correct answer:

main.cpp
vector<long long> ways(6, 0);
ways[0] = 1;
for (int i = 1; i < 6; i++) {
    ways[i] = ways[i - 1] + (i >= 2 ? ways[i - 2] : 0);
}
cout << ways[5] << endl;

questiontext.text:
Match each term with its meaning.

Drag each description onto the item it belongs to.

State  →  [[1]]

Recurrence  →  [[2]]

Memoization  →  [[3]]

Bottom-up  →  [[4]]

Top-down  →  [[5]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. These five words are the core vocabulary of dynamic programming.

The correct answer:

  • State → The description of one subproblem
  • Recurrence → An equation linking a state to smaller states
  • Memoization → Saving an answer after the first computation
  • Bottom-up → Filling a table from small states to big ones
  • Top-down → Recursion that reads saved answers

questiontext.text:
Sort each description: top-down or bottom-up?

Drag the correct label next to every item.

A recursive function that checks a memo array first  →  [[1]]

A for loop that fills dp from index 2 upward  →  [[2]]

It may need a deep call stack  →  [[1]]

It starts from the base cases and climbs  →  [[2]]

It computes only the states that are asked for  →  [[1]]

It computes every smaller state in order  →  [[2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. Top-down starts from the question and recurses, saving answers as it goes. Bottom-up starts from the base cases and fills a table with a loop.

The correct answer:

Top-down (notebook): A recursive function that checks a memo array first, It may need a deep call stack, It computes only the states that are asked for
Bottom-up (table): A for loop that fills dp from index 2 upward, It starts from the base cases and climbs, It computes every smaller state in order

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

vector<long long> memo;
long long calls = 0;

long long fib(int n) {
    calls++;
    if (n < 2) {
        return n;
    }
    if (memo[n] != -1) {
        return memo[n];
    }
    memo[n] = fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);
    return memo[n];
}

int main() {
    memo.assign(7, -1);
    fib(6);
    cout << calls << endl;
    return 0;
}

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. With the notebook each state is computed once and every other request is a single call that reads the notebook, so fib(6) needs 2 x 6 - 1 = 11 calls. The plain solution would need 25.
